course.title: Web Development and Application Engineering
course.short_description: Learn responsive CSS, practical JavaScript, and modern React frontend development through guided lessons and projects.
course.long_description: This section of Web Development and Application Engineering takes learners from CSS fundamentals through JavaScript interactions and component-based React applications. Learners build responsive layouts, reason about data and browser events, and organize maintainable frontend interfaces. Each lesson includes teaching material, a worked example, a guided activity, an independent exercise, and answer-keyed knowledge checks.

lessons.title: CSS Fundamentals and Selectors
lessons.description: CSS rules, external stylesheets, type, class, ID and descendant selectors, pseudo-classes, cascade, specificity and inheritance.
lessons.content_markdown:
# CSS Fundamentals and Selectors

## Learning objectives
Learners will explain and apply the concepts in this lesson, build a working example, test it, and diagnose a common mistake.

## Lesson explanation
CSS rules, external stylesheets, type, class, ID and descendant selectors, pseudo-classes, cascade, specificity and inheritance.

Read the worked example. Identify the input, the rule or logic being applied, and the visible result. Change one value at a time and predict the result before running the code. This develops debugging skills and prevents copy-and-paste learning.

## Worked example
```css
.page { max-width: 60rem; margin: 0 auto; padding: 2rem; }
.page__title { color: #17324d; }
nav a:hover, nav a:focus-visible { text-decoration: underline; }
```

## Guided activity
Build a profile card using an external stylesheet, reusable classes, a descendant selector, and visible hover and keyboard-focus states.

Link styles.css; style the heading with .profile__title; style paragraphs with p; style links inside nav; add hover and focus-visible rules.

Use browser developer tools or development-server output to check for errors. Record what you changed and why.

## Practical engineering notes
- Prefer clear names and small, focused rules or functions.
- Test the expected path and at least one edge case.
- Keep accessibility, readable structure and maintainability in mind.
- Never treat user-provided input as trusted HTML or trusted server data.

## Knowledge check
1. Define the central concept in this lesson and explain why it is useful.
2. Identify the part of the example that controls the behaviour or presentation.
3. Describe one likely beginner error and how you would diagnose it.
4. Name one edge case or accessibility concern that should be tested.
5. Explain how you would improve the example if the application became larger.

## Completion criteria
- The worked example is understood and successfully run.
- The guided activity is completed and tested.
- The independent exercise is submitted.
- The learner can explain key implementation decisions without relying only on copied code.
lessons.exercise:
--- QUESTION ---

Build a profile card using an external stylesheet, reusable classes, a descendant selector, and visible hover and keyboard-focus states.

1. Complete the implementation described above.
2. Test the normal user flow and one edge case.
3. Submit the source code and a short explanation of your decisions.
4. Identify one improvement you would make before production use.

--- SOLUTION ---

Use <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">. Apply .profile__title { color: #17324d; }, p { line-height: 1.6; }, nav a { text-decoration: none; }, and nav a:hover, nav a:focus-visible { text-decoration: underline; }.

Equivalent implementations are acceptable when they meet the requirements and handle the stated edge case.

# Colors, Typography, Spacing, and Layout

## Learning objectives

## Worked example
```css
* { box-sizing: border-box; }
:root { --ink: #172b3a; --muted: #526574; --space: 1rem; }
body { color: var(--ink); font: 1rem/1.6 system-ui, sans-serif; }
.card { max-width: 42rem; margin: 2rem auto; padding: 1.5rem; border: 1px solid #d7e0e7; }
```

- Keep accessibility, readable structure and maintainability in mind.
- Never treat user-provided input as trusted HTML or trusted server data.

2. Identify the part of the example that controls the behaviour or presentation.
3. Describe one likely beginner error and how you would diagnose it.

# Flexbox and CSS Grid

## Learning objectives
Learners will explain and apply the concepts in this lesson, build a working example, test it, and diagnose a common mistake.

## Lesson explanation
Flexbox main and cross axes, alignment, wrapping, gap, Grid rows and columns, repeat(), minmax() and responsive tracks.

Read the worked example. Identify the input, the rule or logic being applied, and the visible result. Change one value at a time and predict the result before running the code. This develops debugging skills and prevents copy-and-paste learning.

## Worked example
```css
.toolbar { display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: space-between; gap: 1rem; flex-wrap: wrap; }
.cards { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(14rem, 1fr)); gap: 1rem; }
```

## Guided activity
Build a three-card course catalogue. Use Flexbox for the header and Grid for the cards. Test long labels and narrow widths.

Align brand and navigation with Flexbox; create cards with Grid and minmax(); use gap instead of child margins; test wide, medium and narrow widths.

- Test the expected path and at least one edge case.
- Keep accessibility, readable structure and maintainability in mind.
- Never treat user-provided input as trusted HTML or trusted server data.

2. Identify the part of the example that controls the behaviour or presentation.
3. Describe one likely beginner error and how you would diagnose it.

# Responsive Design and Mobile-First Development

## Learning objectives
Learners will explain and apply the concepts in this lesson, build a working example, test it, and diagnose a common mistake.

## Lesson explanation

Read the worked example. Identify the input, the rule or logic being applied, and the visible result. Change one value at a time and predict the result before running the code. This develops debugging skills and prevents copy-and-paste learning.

## Worked example
```css
.page { width: min(100% - 2rem, 70rem); margin-inline: auto; }
.hero { display: grid; gap: 1.5rem; }
.hero img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; }
@media (min-width: 48rem) {
  .hero { grid-template-columns: 1.2fr 1fr; }
```

# Data Types, Conditions, and Loops

## Learning objectives
Learners will explain and apply the concepts in this lesson, build a working example, test it, and diagnose a common mistake.

## Lesson explanation
Primitive and reference types, strict equality, truthy and falsy values, if/else, for, while, for...of and input validation.

Read the worked example. Identify the input, the rule or logic being applied, and the visible result. Change one value at a time and predict the result before running the code. This develops debugging skills and prevents copy-and-paste learning.

## Worked example
```javascript
const scores = [72, 88, 49, 95];
let total = 0;
let passCount = 0;
for (const score of scores) {
  total += score;
  if (score >= 50) passCount += 1;
}
const average = scores.length ? total / scores.length : null;
console.log({ passCount, average });
```

## Guided activity
Write a score analyser that counts passing scores of 50 or higher and calculates an average. Define safe behaviour for an empty array.

Create five numeric scores; iterate with for...of; count passing scores; guard against division by zero; print count and average.

Use browser developer tools or development-server output to check for errors. Record what you changed and why.

## Practical engineering notes
- Prefer clear names and small, focused rules or functions.
- Test the expected path and at least one edge case.
- Keep accessibility, readable structure and maintainability in mind.
- Never treat user-provided input as trusted HTML or trusted server data.

## Knowledge check
1. Define the central concept in this lesson and explain why it is useful.
2. Identify the part of the example that controls the behaviour or presentation.
3. Describe one likely beginner error and how you would diagnose it.
4. Name one edge case or accessibility concern that should be tested.
5. Explain how you would improve the example if the application became larger.

## Completion criteria
- The worked example is understood and successfully run.
- The guided activity is completed and tested.
- The independent exercise is submitted.
- The learner can explain key implementation decisions without relying only on copied code.

2. Test the normal user flow and one edge case.

4. Identify one improvement you would make before production use.

--- SOLUTION ---

# Functions, Arrays, and Objects

## Learning objectives

## Worked example
```javascript
const tasks = [{ id: 1, title: "Read CSS", done: true }, { id: 2, title: "Practise JS", done: false }];
const openTasks = items => items.filter(task => !task.done);
const titles = openTasks(tasks).map(task => task.title);
console.log(titles);
```

## Guided activity
Model learning tasks as objects. Write functions to add a task, find a task by ID and return incomplete tasks. Explain which operations mutate the original array.

Create task objects; filter incomplete tasks; find a task by ID; return a new array with an added task using spread syntax.

- Prefer clear names and small, focused rules or functions.
- Test the expected path and at least one edge case.
- Keep accessibility, readable structure and maintainability in mind.
- Never treat user-provided input as trusted HTML or trusted server data.

lessons.title: Props, State, and User Interactions
lessons.description: Read-only props, useState, state setters, functional updates, immutable array/object updates, controlled event handlers and state ownership.
lessons.content_markdown:
# Props, State, and User Interactions

## Learning objectives
Learners will explain and apply the concepts in this lesson, build a working example, test it, and diagnose a common mistake.

## Lesson explanation
Read-only props, useState, state setters, functional updates, immutable array/object updates, controlled event handlers and state ownership.

Read the worked example. Identify the input, the rule or logic being applied, and the visible result. Change one value at a time and predict the result before running the code. This develops debugging skills and prevents copy-and-paste learning.

## Worked example
```javascript
import { useState } from "react";
function ProgressButton({ initialCount = 0 }) {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(initialCount);
  return <button onClick={() => setCount(current => current + 1)}>
    Completed lessons: {count}
  </button>;
}
```

## Guided activity
Build a progress widget receiving learnerName as a prop and tracking completed lessons with state. Add increment and reset actions.

Accept learnerName; initialize completed count with useState(0); increment with a functional update; add reset; display learner name.

Use browser developer tools or development-server output to check for errors. Record what you changed and why.

## Practical engineering notes
- Prefer clear names and small, focused rules or functions.
- Test the expected path and at least one edge case.
- Keep accessibility, readable structure and maintainability in mind.
- Never treat user-provided input as trusted HTML or trusted server data.

## Knowledge check
1. Define the central concept in this lesson and explain why it is useful.
2. Identify the part of the example that controls the behaviour or presentation.
3. Describe one likely beginner error and how you would diagnose it.
4. Name one edge case or accessibility concern that should be tested.
5. Explain how you would improve the example if the application became larger.

## Completion criteria
- The worked example is understood and successfully run.
- The guided activity is completed and tested.
- The independent exercise is submitted.
- The learner can explain key implementation decisions without relying only on copied code.

practice_questions.prompt: What makes a React input controlled?
options: Its value is driven by state and updated by an event handler
